JSON: Name: vietnam_logistics_three_layer_mcdm Title: Performance evaluation of listed Vietnamese logistics companies across pre-, during-, and post-COVID-19 periods using a three-layer multi-criteria decision-making framework Short Hypothesis: A three-layer MCDM framework that separately aggregates financial, operational, and market criteria produces company rankings that differ significantly (p < 0.05) from rankings produced by conventional single-layer MCDM approaches, and these differences capture systematic shifts between pre-, during-, and post-COVID-19 periods. Related Work: Existing research applies multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques—such as TOPSIS, EDAS, AHP (and fuzzy variants), CRITIC-based objective weighting, and DEA/Malmquist efficiency analysis—to corporate performance evaluation and logistics-sector assessment. Integrated pipelines combine objective weighting (e.g., CRITIC) with distance-based rankers (TOPSIS, EDAS) or with fuzzy/interval extensions to handle uncertainty. Other approaches rely on DEA for efficiency measurement or use time-series Malmquist indices to capture dynamics. Limitations across prior work include reliance on single-layer criteria aggregation (mixing heterogeneous metrics without hierarchical structuring), subjective or inconsistent weighting choices, sensitivity to normalization and outliers, limited validation against ex-post market outcomes, sparse treatment of temporal regime shifts (e.g., pandemic phases), and small or single-country samples that restrict generalizability. Few studies systematically compare multi-layered hierarchical aggregation to single-layer baselines or quantify how such structuring affects sensitivity to crisis-induced performance changes. Abstract: This research addresses robust comparative performance evaluation of listed Vietnamese logistics firms across pre-, during-, and post-COVID-19 periods. We propose a three-layer multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) framework that organizes indicators into a hierarchical structure of criterion domains (financial, operational, market), subcriteria, and observable metrics, and uses objective weighting at each layer to produce composite rankings per period. The main contribution is an empirical assessment of whether hierarchical aggregation improves detection of pandemic-driven performance shifts and yields rankings that better align with ex-post market and distress signals than conventional single-layer MCDM alternatives. Expected outcomes include (1) quantification of ranking differences across periods attributable to the three-layer structure, (2) evaluation of alignment between MCDM-derived ranks and financial/market outcomes, and (3) sensitivity and ablation analyses that reveal which layers/subcriteria drive ranking changes. The study informs practitioners and researchers on hierarchical MCDM design choices for crisis-aware corporate performance assessment. Experiments: Datasets: consolidated annual and quarterly financial statements, operational metrics, and market data for all Vietnamese logistics firms listed on VNDirect/HOSE/HNX from 2018–2024; data sources: company filings, Vietnam General Statistics Office, Ministry reports, and stock-exchange records. Partition periods: pre-COVID-19 = 2018–2019, during-COVID-19 = 2020–2021, post-COVID-19 = 2022–2024. Expected sample size: all firms continuously or intermittently listed in that window (N ≈ 15–40 firms), with firm-period observations. Preprocessing: winsorize outliers at 1st/99th percentiles; impute missing scalar entries via median by industry-quarter; normalize metrics using range and z-score variants per experiment. Proposed method: three-layer MCDM with objective weighting (layer-wise CRITIC) and distance/utility aggregation to produce period-specific ranks. Baselines: (1) single-layer CRITIC+TOPSIS, (2) single-layer CRITIC+EDAS, (3) fuzzy-AHP+TOPSIS (subjective weights), (4) DEA-Malmquist efficiency scores. Evaluation metrics: Spearman rank correlation, Kendall's tau, mean absolute rank change, rank stability index, alignment with ex-post outcomes measured by (a) 12-month forward stock return ranking correlation, (b) Tobin's Q and Altman Z-score correlation, (c) bankruptcy/delinquency binary classification AUC. Statistical tests: Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired rank differences, permutation tests for rank correlation significance (α = 0.05). Experimental setup: compute ranks per firm per period for proposed and baseline methods; test hypothesis by comparing distribution of paired rank differences across methods and periods. Ablation studies: (A) remove one layer (financial/operational/market) to measure its contribution, (B) replace objective CRITIC weights with entropy and equal weights, (C) vary normalization (min-max vs z-score) and outlier treatment, (D) vary pandemic boundary windows (alternate splits: 2019–2020 vs 2021–2022). Robustness checks: apply bootstrap resampling of firms (1,000 samples) and recompute rank statistics; sensitivity to missing-data imputation by comparing median vs multiple-imputation outcomes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Small sample size and firm turnover (listings, delistings, mergers) may reduce statistical power and introduce survivorship bias. Accounting policy heterogeneity and reporting lags across firms can bias indicator comparability. Objective-weighting methods (e.g., CRITIC) are sensitive to collinearity, scale, and outliers; normalization choices can substantially change ranks. Market-based validation (stock returns, Tobin's Q) is endogenous to firm performance and may conflate market sentiment with underlying operations. Temporal partitioning choices may misclassify period effects for firms with atypical timelines. DEA and efficiency baselines require larger cross-sectional samples to be stable. The proposed framework yields associative, not causal, inferences about pandemic effects. Generalization is limited to listed Vietnamese logistics companies and to the specific metric set used; transfer to other sectors or unlisted firms may not hold. Computational cost is modest but increases with bootstrap and imputation ensembles; real-time or very high-frequency application is not assessed.
